articles.title: Problem Statements and the Scope of Prior Art
articles.content:
专利法中"显而易见性"原则自1952年确立以来，要求发明不仅仅是"新的"，还必须相对于现有技术有实质性的技术进步。核心问题在于一个领域内普通技术人员（POSITA）在专利申请时是否会认为该发明是现有技术的显而易见延伸。在进行事后分析时，首先需要考虑相关的先前技术，即法律上称为"类似"技术。先前技术属于类似技术的条件是：1）与所申请专利属于同一技术领域；或2）与发明者试图解决的特定问题相关。非类似技术则不纳入显而易见性分析范围。

资深的专利律师通常在起草专利文本时通过精细定义技术领域和问题范围来影响类似技术的认定。然而，根据联邦巡回法院近日判决，这种起草策略可能无效，特别是当专利权利要求本身起草过于宽泛时。

在《尼尔森公司（美国）有限责任公司诉TVision Insights公司》案中（案号2025-1371，2026年8月14日），法院维持了专利审查试验庭（PTAB）取消尼尔森公司电视观众测量相关专利（US11470243）的最终决定。该专利使用摄像头技术进行观众测量。尼尔森公司辩称，一篇关于面部表情分析的科学论文不属于类似技术，因为其专利说明书明确指出发明人面临的问题是：频繁激活照明源导致"显著耗电"，缩短灯的使用寿命，产生热量，并打扰被观察者。尽管说明书明确指出了问题，但审查试验庭将问题定义得更为广泛，即图像处理和面部检测，联邦巡回法院认定这一认定有充分证据支持。

尼尔森公司的问题在于其权利要求范围远超说明书中描述的问题。实际上，受质疑的权利要求并未提及光源或其消除。由于权利要求范围超出了照明问题的范畴，上诉庭认为"在权利要求本身并未限定光源存在的情况下，将相关问题限制为减少光源使用是不恰当的"。

法院援引KSR案判例："无论是专利权人的特定动机还是声称的目的都不控制性。关键在于权利要求的客观范围。"KSR国际公司诉Teleflex公司案（2007年）。尽管KSR案侧重于结合动机而非类似技术，但许多法官认为该案为两者提供了灵活性，允许考虑更多先前技术。

本案的教训在于：说明书中狭窄的问题陈述无法挽救过于宽泛的权利要求。这提醒申请人在起草专利时，权利要求的范围应与说明书中问题陈述保持一致，避免因范围过广而引发显而易见性争议。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

A patentable invention needs to be more than simply "new."  Rather, an invention  requires a substantial step beyond what was already known in the field.  Since 1952, this doctrine has been known as "obviousness," and the core question is whether a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) would have - at the time of the patent  application filing - seen the invention as an obvious extension.  A key first step in this hindsight analysis is to look at the relevant prior art - the legal term is "analogous" art.  A prior art reference is analogous if it is either (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention or (2) is reasonably pertinent to the particular problem the inventor was trying to solve.  Non-analogous art is not considered for obviousness purposes.

Savvy patent attorneys have attempted to shape this test somewhat in the patent drafting process by narrowly defining the field as well as the problem being solved.

But, as the Federal Circuit explained this week, those drafting choices are not controlling, particularly when the claims themselves are broadly drafted.

In Nielsen Co. (US), LLC v. TVision Insights, Inc., No. 2025-1371 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 14, 2026), the court affirmed a PTAB final written decision cancelling claims of Nielsen's camera-based television audience measurement patent US11470243.  Nielsen argued that a scientific paper on facial expression analysis was not analogous art because its patent specification had expressly identified the problem facing its inventor: frequent activation of the illumination source, which causes a "significant power drain," shortens the lamp's lifetime, generates heat, and annoys the people being watched.  Despite that express statement, the Board had identified the problem differently and more broadly, as one of image processing and facial detection, and the Federal Circuit held that substantial evidence supported that finding.

Nielsen's problem is that its claims were much broader than its problem statement.  In fact, the challenged claims did not recite a light source or its elimination. Because the claims reached well past the stated illumination problem, the appellate panel found that it would be "inappropriate to limit the relevant problem to reducing light-source use when the claims themselves are not limited to the presence of a light source."

The court quoted KSR: "neither the particular motivation nor the avowed purpose of the patentee controls. What matters is the objective reach of the claim." KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007).  Although KSR was focused on motivation-to-combine rather than analogous-arts, many have seen that case as providing flexibility to both doctrines to allow consideration of more art.

The ultimate lesson here: A narrow problem statement in the specification will not save broad claims.
